new_statements.translation: 2.1.2. Stress is dynamic and word-level; it may fall on any syllable: muşåt 'beautiful', mére 'to go', ócniţe 'little window', clópotele 'the bells' (with definite article). In the verbal paradigm stress is mobile, so that it can serve to distinguish word forms: adurå 'to bring' — adúra 'brings'. In connected speech only content words bear stress; function words are unstressed, so the delimitative function of stress is weakly expressed.
new_statements.citation: Narumov, B. P. 2001. Istrorumynskij jazyk/dialekt. In I. I. Čelyševa, B. P. Narumov, O. I. Romanova (eds.), Jazyki mira: Romanskie jazyki, 656–671. Moskva: Academia.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check:, PDF page 661 = printed p. 660 (running head 'Романские языки'), §2.1.2. extracted text gives the Russian text of the quoted paragraph word for word ('Ударение силовое, словесное, может падать на любой слог.. В парадигме глагольного спряжения ударение подвижное.. adurå — adúra.. служебные слова безударны, поэтому делимитативная функция ударения выражена слабо'); the Latin-script examples are garbled in the text, so I rendered the page at 200 dpi and read them from the image: muşåt 'красивый', mére 'идти', ócniţe 'окошко', clópotele 'колокола' (с опред. артиклем), adurå 'приносить' — adúra 'приносит' — exactly as the compilers transcribed. Verbatim confirmed. Identity: the chapt…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Free (lexically/morphologically determined) dynamic word stress of the Romanian type: it can stand on the final, penultimate, antepenultimate or earlier syllable; it is mobile within verb paradigms and can be the sole distinction between forms; clitics/function words are unstressed. Hurren's first-hand data (1971: 35–40; 1999: 8–15) independently show prominence on any of the 1st–5th syllables of 2–6-syllable words; Pușcariu 1926 §§109–110 adds that inherited words keep the Romanian accent and Slavic loans are mostly (pen)ult-stressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Narumov says nothing; Pușcariu 1926 §16/§109 mentions a 'ton secundar' on the first syllable of some longer words (e.g. cătra-type forms) but gives no rule; Hurren treats only one prominent syllable per unit.
new_statements.exceptions: Verb paradigms: stress on root in sg/3pl vs on ending in 1–2pl for inherited verbs, always on the person marker for Slavic-origin verbs (Kovačec 1971: 136–137 apud Zegrean 2012); superlative måi vs comparative mai distinguished by stress; phrase stress shifts onto negation nu and onto prepositions (zå-me) on the Croatian model (Pușcariu §111); stress never falls on the enclitic article (Filipi 2005); stressed /a/ realized as [å] in inherited words.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation forms (examples include article-bearing forms like clópotele); Narumov notes that in connected speech only content words carry stress. Description covers both Žejane (northern) and southern (Šušnjevica etc.) varieties without dialect difference in stress placement.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Istro-Romanian as a whole (glottocode istr1245, ISO ruo), covering both the northern Žejane variety (Žejanski) and the southern villages around Šušnjevica (Vlaški); none reports a dialect difference in stress placement. Hurren's data are mainly from Šušnjevica/Nova Vas and Žejane (1966–67 fieldwork); Narumov's sketch is literature-based (chiefly Kovačec 1971, Pușcariu 1926).

sources.note: Reports that Kovačec 1971's phonetics/phonology part (pp. 33–80) treats stressed and unstressed vowels, consonants, clusters 'et enfin l'accent'; superlative måi bur vs comparative mai bur distinguished by accent (K. p. 108).

sources.citation: Hurren, H. A. 1971 [Glottolog: 1972]. A linguistic description of Istro-Rumanian. D.Phil. thesis, University of Oxford (Michaelmas Term 1971). xii+475 pp. ORA uuid:bfb29e35-e2b8-4613-97cf-3b62bdb6a1f6.
sources.note: pp. 35–40 (ch. 1): the 'distributional unit' consists of one prominent (stressed) syllable plus non-prominent syllables 'grouped around it in various combinations'; enumerates 20 types of di- to hexasyllabic units with prominence on 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th or 5th syllable (/vínde/ vs /potók/, /préfTSilor/ vs /galíra/ vs /siromåh/ etc.), i.e. stress position is lexically free; prominent syllable marked with an acute; pp. 166-167 stress shift in 2sg verb forms. No one-sentence placement rule.

sources.citation: Pușcariu, Sextil (with M. Bartoli, A. Belulovici, A. Byhan). 1926. Studii istroromâne II: Introducere – Gramatică – Caracterizarea dialectului istroromân. București: Cultura Națională.
sources.note: §§109–111 'Accentul', pp. 138–139: Latin-origin words keep the old Romanian accent (with a few shifts); Slavic proparoxytones sometimes keep antepenult stress but are usually stressed on the (pen)ult 'după firea limbii române'; mobile accent in nouns in -åț/-ån; accent variation between villages/investigators; phrase accent moves onto negation and (Croatian-style) onto prepositions.

tone.translation: 2. It is known that one of the particularities of the Istro-Romanian dialect consists in the fact that [a] became [å] in stressed syllables. (The only prosodic fact the article uses; it contains no statement on tone.)
